title: Show the wool
hookLine: sheep don't show the shepherd their fodder, they show wool (Enchiridion 46)

cards: Somewhere tonight, someone who just finished a book on mindfulness is explaining it at dinner, while visibly not being mindful. Plenty of people have been that someone.
You've been on this path a long time now, nearly four hundred days, and it would be natural to want to talk about it.
Section forty-six of the handbook has a word for that urge, and then it gives a strange picture: a field of sheep.

teach.b: Never call yourself a philosopher, Epictetus says, and don't talk much about your principles among people who haven't asked. Do what follows from them. At a dinner, don't explain how one ought to eat.
Eat as one ought. Socrates, he says, had so completely given up showing off that people would come to him asking to be introduced to philosophers, and he would take them.
He let himself be overlooked, and didn't mind. Here's the test: when someone tells you that you know nothing, and it doesn't sting, you can know you've begun the work.
And if talk among people new to all this turns to principles, mostly keep quiet. There's a danger, he says, of throwing up what you haven't digested yet. That's not a polite image.
He means it not to be. Then the sheep.
Sheep don't bring their grass back up to show the shepherd how much they've eaten.
They digest the pasture inside, and what comes out is wool and milk.
So don't show people your principles; show them the actions that come from digesting them. Talk is the grass. Practice is the wool.
People can't use your grass. They can use your wool: a moment of patience, a gossip skipped, a promise kept without swearing.
After nearly four hundred days, a good sign of this path may be something someone else notices in you, without you ever mentioning where it came from.

how: Some people practicing Stoicism avoid calling themselves Stoics or explaining philosophy uninvited, and try to let it show in how they act instead.

o: what you digest quietly, so it comes out as action
the duty to guide others who are still learning
a quiet retreat where you rest from the world

games.q: show the wool — tap the pairs.
p: eat as one ought, don't explain
the actions that come from them

s: Epictetus encourages students to call themselves philosophers
never call yourself one, he says. do what follows from the principles.
people asked Socrates to introduce them to philosophers
and he took them, content to be overlooked.
sheep, in Epictetus' picture, show the shepherd how much grass they ate
they digest it and produce wool and milk.

games.q: at dinner, a friend asks why you skipped dessert. what fits Enchiridion 46?
o: give a short talk on Stoic self-control.
say something simple, and let the practice speak.
games.why: don't explain how one ought to eat; eat as one ought. show the wool, not the grass.

practice: Look back over this path, the words, the stories, the practices, and find one thing that has actually changed in how you live: not something you could explain, something you do, like a pause before reacting, a smaller portion, a kinder answer.
That's your wool. Hold it quietly, without a word about where it came from.

wordCard.voice: Pasture. What a sheep digests quietly inside, giving back wool and milk, not the grass itself; show practice, not principles. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a sheep, Epictetus' picture of digesting principles into wool and milk.

carryVoice: Your line: practice is the wool. Grass is for digesting; wool is for giving. That's day three hundred eighty-one.
